instruction: Please implement a website for generating stock reports to provide stock information and analysis. The website should have the functionality to search and summarize stock information, and generate customized stock reports based on user requirements. Users should be able to input stock codes or names, select report formats and content, and the website will automatically generate the corresponding reports. The reports should include basic stock information, market trends, financial data, and more. Set the background color to white and the component color to navy.

ui_instruct.task: Verify the stock search functionality by entering a valid stock code.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system returns relevant stock information and analysis corresponding to the entered stock code, displaying details such as basic stock information, market trends, and financial data.

ui_instruct.task: Test the report customization feature by selecting different report formats and content options.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system provides options for various report formats and content customization, enabling users to choose according to their preferences.

ui_instruct.task: Input a stock name instead of a stock code to search for stock information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website successfully recognizes the stock name, retrieving and displaying the relevant stock information and analysis.

ui_instruct.task: Generate a customized stock report by choosing specific elements to include (e.g., market trends, financial data).
ui_instruct.expected_result: The generated report correctly includes the selected elements, accurately reflecting the user's specified choices.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate through the website and test all buttons function correctly by clicking each of them and back to the homepage.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Each click on a button leads to the appropriate page or action without any errors, ensuring smooth navigation.

ui_instruct.task: Evaluate the website's form inputs by submitting incomplete or incorrect stock information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system displays appropriate error messages and guidance on how to correct the input errors, ensuring robust input validation.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'white' as the background color and 'navy' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'white' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'navy', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.instruction: Before we go further, pin down a demo universe so we're always looking at the same numbers — exactly these eight stocks, I'll add more later: Argent Micro (ARGN, Technology, $84.50, P/E 31.4, market cap $142B, yield 0.0%), Baltic Freight (BLTC, Industrials, $23.75, P/E 9.8, $8B, 4.2%), Comet Energy (CMET, Energy, $61.20, P/E 12.6, $54B, 5.1%), Driftwood Retail (DRFT, Consumer Goods, $9.15, P/E 22.0, $2B, 1.8%), Ember Semiconductor (EMBR, Technology, $147.30, P/E 41.7, $210B, 0.4%), Fjord Pharma (FJRD, Healthcare, $33.60, P/E 12.6, $18B, 2.5%), Greenline Utilities (GRNL, Utilities, $54.80, P/E 15.5, $27B, 3.9%), and Helix Software (HLXS, Technology, $58.90, P/E 27.3, $65B, 1.1%). Then give me a proper screener page: sector checkboxes where a stock passes if it's in any checked sector, typed boxes for maximum P/E and minimum dividend yield that all have to hold together, a live 'X of 8 match' readout that follows every change, and sortable columns where a P/E sort breaks ties alphabetically by ticker. Clicking a result row should drop me straight into generating that stock's report. I also want two built-in presets — 'Dividend Payers' for yield of at least 2.5% and 'Cheap Tech' for Technology under P/E 35 — plus the ability to save my own named presets and re-run them later. House rule from here on out: every percentage anywhere in this app, yields today or any gains and weights we ever add, shows one decimal with the % sign, like 4.2%, never 4.20% or 4%.
follow_ups.source_feature: Equity screener with multi-criteria filtering (fused with Simply Wall St's curated investing themes as built-in presets)

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, check the Technology and Healthcare sector boxes and type 1.0 into the minimum dividend yield box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Only Fjord Pharma and Helix Software remain in the results — Argent Micro and Ember Semiconductor are excluded for low yield — and the match readout says 2 of 8.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, clear any active filters, then sort the results by the P/E column in ascending order.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The first three rows are Baltic Freight (9.8), Comet Energy (12.6), then Fjord Pharma (12.6) — the 12.6 tie is broken alphabetically by ticker, so CMET comes before FJRD.

ui_instruct.task: Click the built-in 'Dividend Payers' preset on the screener.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Results show exactly Baltic Freight, Comet Energy, Fjord Pharma, and Greenline Utilities — the boundary stock Fjord Pharma at exactly 2.5% is included.

ui_instruct.task: Click the Comet Energy row in the screener results.
ui_instruct.expected_result: You land in report generation with Comet Energy pre-selected, and generating produces the report for Comet Energy.

ui_instruct.task: Type CMET into the stock search and generate a report with all content options selected.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A report for the searched stock appears, including basic stock information, market trends, and financial data sections.

follow_ups.instruction: That screener is already paying off — now I need somewhere to keep candidates. Add a Watchlist page with two groups, Core and Speculative; start it with Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma in Core and Helix Software in Speculative, and put a note on Fjord Pharma that says 'watch Q3 margins'. I want an add-to-watchlist button with a group picker on every screener result row and on any generated report, and if a stock is already on the list don't create a second row — just tell me it's already saved. On the watchlist itself let me edit notes, move a stock between groups, and remove entries. One more house style going forward: any time a stock appears anywhere in this app, show its ticker in a small navy badge in front of the name, like [FJRD] Fjord Pharma — everywhere, including whatever we build later.
follow_ups.source_feature: Smart alerts and watchlist notifications (the watchlist half, extended with groups and notes)

ui_instruct.task: Open the Watchlist page on a fresh load.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The Core group shows Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma, Speculative shows Helix Software, and Fjord Pharma displays the note 'watch Q3 margins'.

ui_instruct.task: From the screener results, click the add-to-watchlist control on the Comet Energy row and choose the Core group, then open the Watchlist page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: No duplicate is created — the watchlist still has exactly three entries with a single Comet Energy row, and the app indicates it was already saved.

ui_instruct.task: On the Watchlist, move Helix Software from Speculative to Core.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Helix Software now appears under Core alongside the other two stocks and no longer appears under Speculative.

ui_instruct.task: In the screener, click add-to-watchlist on the Greenline Utilities row, choose Speculative, then open the Watchlist page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Greenline Utilities appears under the Speculative group on the watchlist.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, clear any active filters, then sort the results by the P/E column in ascending order.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The first three rows are Baltic Freight (9.8), Comet Energy (12.6), then Fjord Pharma (12.6) — the 12.6 tie is broken alphabetically by ticker, so CMET comes before FJRD.

follow_ups.instruction: Let's make the watchlist talk money: add a Positions view where every watchlisted stock gets a shares box and a buy-price box, and everything recalculates as I type — market value at the stock's price, gain or loss in dollars and percent, each position's weight of the whole portfolio, and a totals row. Load my real positions to start: 50 CMET bought at $48.00, 100 FJRD at $36.50, and 45 HLXS at $52.25. Weights are one decimal but they must always total exactly 100.0% — when plain rounding leaves you at 99.9 or 100.1, adjust the weight that was closest to rounding the other way. A blank or zero shares box just drops that row out of the totals with no NaN or error anywhere, and negative numbers get rejected. Also a default for the whole app from here on: any list of stocks where I haven't picked a sort shows alphabetically by ticker.
follow_ups.source_feature: Smart alerts and watchlist notifications (watchlist extended into live portfolio position tracking)

ui_instruct.task: Open the Positions view on a fresh load and read the weight column.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Fjord Pharma's weight reads 37.1% (not 37.0%), so the three weights 33.7%, 37.1%, and 29.2% total exactly 100.0%, and total market value shows $9,070.50.

ui_instruct.task: In the Positions view, change Comet Energy's shares from 50 to 60.
ui_instruct.expected_result: After entering 60, CMET's market value updates to $3,672.00 without any save button, the totals row recalculates immediately, and the three weights still add up to exactly 100.0%.

ui_instruct.task: Clear Helix Software's shares box so it is empty.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The HLXS row drops out of the totals — total market value becomes $6,420.00 for the two remaining positions, no NaN or error appears, and the two remaining weights still total exactly 100.0%.

ui_instruct.task: Add Baltic Freight to the watchlist from the screener, then open the Positions view and type 10 into Baltic Freight's shares box and 20.00 into its buy price box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Baltic Freight appears as a position row and shows market value $237.50 with a gain of +18.8%.

ui_instruct.task: From the screener results, click the add-to-watchlist control on the Comet Energy row and choose the Core group, then open the Watchlist page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: No duplicate is created — the watchlist still has exactly three entries with a single Comet Energy row, and the app indicates it was already saved.

follow_ups.instruction: Time for the health snapshot I keep sketching on paper. Build a Ratings page that scores all eight stocks 0-5 on five dimensions and stacks them up. Value comes straight off P/E — under 10 is a 5, from 10 up to but not including 15 is a 4, 15 up to 25 is a 3, 25 up to 35 is a 2, and 35 or more is a 1; Dividend comes off yield — exactly zero is 0, under 1% is 1, from 1 up to 2% is 2, 2 up to 3% is 3, 3 up to 4.5% is 4, and 4.5% or better is 5. For Growth, Profitability, and Financial Health use my analyst numbers, in that order: Argent 5/3/4, Baltic 2/4/5, Comet 1/4/3, Driftwood 3/2/2, Ember 5/5/4, Fjord 4/3/4, Greenline 1/3/5, Helix 4/5/3. Show each stock's five scores as a pentagon or radar snapshot with the total out of 25 and a letter grade — 20 or more is A, 16 to 19 is B, 12 to 15 is C, 8 to 11 is D, under 8 is E — and rank the page best total first, breaking ties alphabetically by ticker. While you're at it, add a Health Score option to report generation so a generated report can include that stock's pentagon and grade.
follow_ups.source_feature: Snowflake visual health score

ui_instruct.task: Open the Ratings page and read the ranking from the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Baltic Freight ranks first with a total of 20 and grade A (20 lands on the A boundary, not B), and the three stocks tied at 16 appear in the order Ember Semiconductor, Greenline Utilities, Helix Software.

ui_instruct.task: On the Ratings page, find Greenline Utilities and read its Value and Dividend scores.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Greenline's Value score is 3 (P/E 15.5 falls in the 15-to-25 bucket, not the bucket below) and its Dividend score is 4 (yield 3.9%).

ui_instruct.task: Check Comet Energy's entry on the Ratings page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Comet Energy shows Dividend 5 (yield 5.1% clears the 4.5% bucket), Value 4, a total of 17 with grade B, and all five dimensions visible on its pentagon or radar snapshot.

ui_instruct.task: Generate a report for Baltic Freight with the Health Score section included.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The generated report contains a Health Score section showing Baltic Freight's grade A and total of 20 alongside the other selected report content.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, check the Technology and Healthcare sector boxes and type 1.0 into the minimum dividend yield box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Only Fjord Pharma and Helix Software remain in the results — Argent Micro and Ember Semiconductor are excluded for low yield — and the match readout says 2 of 8.

follow_ups.instruction: Now alerts, so the watchlist watches itself. Any stock on my watchlist can carry alert rules — pick the stock, a metric (price, P/E, or dividend yield), above or below, and a typed threshold — creatable straight from a watchlist row or inside a new Alerts Center, where the stock picker only offers what's on the watchlist. A rule evaluates against the stock's current numbers the moment it's created and again whenever I edit it, and above/below are strict: a value exactly equal to the threshold has NOT triggered. Start me with three rules: CMET price below $65 (that one's live, price is 61.20), FJRD yield above 3%, and HLXS P/E below 25. The Alerts Center shows every rule with a status rollup of how many are triggered versus watching, and a triggered rule can be dismissed into a separate history section with the rollup staying honest the whole time.
follow_ups.source_feature: Smart alerts and watchlist notifications (the alerts half, evaluated against seeded metrics)

ui_instruct.task: Open the Alerts Center on a fresh load.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The CMET price-below-$65 rule shows triggered, the FJRD and HLXS rules show watching, and the rollup reads 1 triggered and 2 watching.

ui_instruct.task: In the Alerts Center, dismiss the triggered Comet Energy rule.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The rule moves out of the active list into the history section, and the triggered count in the rollup decreases by one while the history section now shows it.

ui_instruct.task: In the Alerts Center, edit the Fjord Pharma yield rule's threshold from 3 to 2.5.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The rule still shows watching — Fjord's yield is exactly 2.5%, and 'above' is strict, so an exactly-equal value does not trigger.

ui_instruct.task: On the Watchlist page, use the set-alert control on the Helix Software row to create a rule for price above 50.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The new rule appears in the Alerts Center attached to Helix Software and immediately shows triggered, since 58.90 is strictly above 50.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Positions view on a fresh load and read the weight column.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Fjord Pharma's weight reads 37.1% (not 37.0%), so the three weights 33.7%, 37.1%, and 29.2% total exactly 100.0%, and total market value shows $9,070.50.

follow_ups.instruction: Add an Earnings Call Highlights hub. Give every one of the eight stocks two short canned quotes from their latest earnings calls, but place the words deliberately: 'automation' appears in exactly four quotes — both of Ember Semiconductor's, one of Argent Micro's, one of Helix Software's — 'tariffs' appears only in Baltic Freight's quotes, and no quote anywhere mentions 'crypto'. Then give me a search box that matches live as I type without caring about capitalization, grouping hits by stock with the matched word highlighted, a match count per stock and a grand total, ordered most matches first with ties going alphabetical by ticker. An empty box should just invite me to search, and a term with zero hits gets a clear no-results note, never a blank screen. While you're in there, let report generation include an Earnings Highlights section carrying that stock's quotes.
follow_ups.source_feature: Transcript keyword search

ui_instruct.task: Type automation into the earnings highlights search box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Three stocks appear in the order Ember Semiconductor (2 matches), Argent Micro (1 match), Helix Software (1 match) — most matches first, the 1-1 tie alphabetical by ticker — with a grand total of 4 and every occurrence of 'automation' highlighted.

ui_instruct.task: Type crypto into the earnings highlights search box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A clear no-results message appears — no crash and no blank results area — and any total shown reads zero.

ui_instruct.task: Type TARIFFS in capital letters into the earnings highlights search box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Baltic Freight's matching quote appears despite the different capitalization, and Baltic Freight is the only stock listed.

ui_instruct.task: Type automation into the search box and look at how each result stock is labeled.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Each result group shows the ticker in a small navy badge in front of the company name — [EMBR] Ember Semiconductor, [ARGN] Argent Micro, [HLXS] Helix Software.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Ratings page and read the ranking from the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Baltic Freight ranks first with a total of 20 and grade A (20 lands on the A boundary, not B), and the three stocks tied at 16 appear in the order Ember Semiconductor, Greenline Utilities, Helix Software.

follow_ups.instruction: I keep flipping between reports to weigh stocks against each other — build me a Compare tool instead. Let me pick two to four stocks and get side-by-side columns with rows for price, market cap, P/E, dividend yield, and the overall health total from the ratings work, recomputing instantly every time I add or drop a stock. Best in row gets highlighted — lowest P/E wins, highest yield wins, highest health total wins — and a genuine tie highlights every stock that shares it. Top it with a win tally per stock counting how many rows it won, with ties counting for everyone in them; if only one stock or none is selected, show a friendly prompt to pick more rather than an empty or broken grid.
follow_ups.source_feature: Snowflake visual health score (fused with Koyfin's screener metrics into a side-by-side comparison grid)

ui_instruct.task: In the Compare tool, select Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The P/E row highlights both columns (each is 12.6), dividend yield highlights Comet Energy (5.1% vs 2.5%), health score highlights Fjord Pharma (18 vs 17), and the win tally reads 2 for Comet Energy and 2 for Fjord Pharma.

ui_instruct.task: With Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma selected, add Baltic Freight as a third stock.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Highlights recompute instantly: Baltic Freight now solely wins P/E (9.8, so the 12.6 pair loses its highlight) and health (20), Comet Energy keeps yield, and the tally reads Baltic 2, Comet 1, Fjord 0.

ui_instruct.task: Remove selected stocks until only one remains.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Instead of a one-column grid or an error, a friendly prompt appears asking to pick at least two stocks to compare.

ui_instruct.task: Select Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma and look at the dividend yield row.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Yields display with exactly one decimal and a % sign — 5.1% and 2.5% — never 5.10% or 5%.

ui_instruct.task: In the Alerts Center, edit the Fjord Pharma yield rule's threshold from 3 to 2.5.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The rule still shows watching — Fjord's yield is exactly 2.5%, and 'above' is strict, so an exactly-equal value does not trigger.

follow_ups.instruction: Facelift time, Koyfin style. Put a light/dark toggle in the header of every page: dark mode swaps to deep navy (#0B1B33) backgrounds with light text, and the choice has to stick as I move between pages. In both themes the primary action buttons — generate report, run or apply a screen, add to watchlist, save an alert — go amber (#F0A92D) with dark navy text; page titles and section headings go uppercase with wide letter-spacing; and every card or panel gets 12px rounded corners with a thin visible border. Keep the ticker badges readable in dark mode too — give them a lighter fill or an outline so they don't vanish into the background. This applies across the whole app — the report page, the screener, the watchlist, the ratings page, the alerts center, all of it, no half-done pages.
follow_ups.source_feature: Customizable workspace themes and layout (light/dark theming)

ui_instruct.task: Click the theme toggle on the screener page, then navigate to the Watchlist page and then the Alerts Center.
ui_instruct.expected_result: All three pages render with the deep navy background and light text — the dark theme persists across navigation with no page left on the light background.

ui_instruct.task: In light mode, look at the primary generate button on the report page and the apply/run control on the screener.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both are amber with dark navy text and match each other, and nearby page titles or section headings render uppercase with wide letter-spacing.

ui_instruct.task: Switch to dark mode and open the Ratings page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page is dark-themed and still ranks Baltic Freight first with grade A and a total of 20 — the restyle did not break the ratings order.

ui_instruct.task: In dark mode, open the Watchlist page and check the Fjord Pharma entry.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The watchlist cards show 12px rounded corners with a visible border on the dark background, the FJRD ticker badge is still legible, and the note 'watch Q3 margins' still displays.

ui_instruct.task: Type automation into the earnings highlights search box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Three stocks appear in the order Ember Semiconductor (2 matches), Argent Micro (1 match), Helix Software (1 match) — most matches first, the 1-1 tie alphabetical by ticker — with a grand total of 4 and every occurrence of 'automation' highlighted.

follow_ups.instruction: Bring it all home with a Command Center as the landing view — one glance, four tiles. A Portfolio tile with total market value and overall gain from my positions, an Alerts tile showing how many rules are currently triggered out of the total, a Top Rated tile naming the stock with the best overall health score and its grade, and a Watchlist tile with the count per group. Every tile is a shortcut to its page, and the numbers can never go stale — if I dismiss an alert or change a share count and come back, the tiles have to reflect it. And on a clean first load it should already be populated from everything we've seeded, not zeros or placeholders.
follow_ups.source_feature: Customizable workspace themes and layout (the dashboard-panel workspace, reshaped into a live rollup command center)

ui_instruct.expected_result: You land on the Positions view with the three seeded positions visible.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The Portfolio tile's total now reads $9,682.50 — the tile recomputed instead of showing the stale $9,070.50.

ui_instruct.task: In the Alerts Center, dismiss the triggered Comet Energy rule, then return to the Command Center.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The Alerts tile now shows 0 triggered, consistent with the Alerts Center rollup after the dismissal.

ui_instruct.task: In the Compare tool, select Comet Energy and Fjord Pharma.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The P/E row highlights both columns (each is 12.6), dividend yield highlights Comet Energy (5.1% vs 2.5%), health score highlights Fjord Pharma (18 vs 17), and the win tally reads 2 for Comet Energy and 2 for Fjord Pharma.

target_app_summary: What began as a simple stock-report generator has grown into a full retail-research workstation over a fixed eight-stock demo universe. A multi-criteria screener with built-in and saved presets feeds a grouped watchlist, which in turn powers a live portfolio positions calculator and a strict-threshold alerts workflow; a five-dimension health-score ratings engine flows into generated reports, a side-by-side compare grid, and the landing Command Center that rolls up portfolio value, alert status, top rating, and watchlist counts. Orthogonal growth includes an earnings-call transcript keyword search wired into report sections and a full light/dark theming pass across every surface. The feature graph runs one chain four deep (base app, then screener, then watchlist, then positions, then command center), with the ratings and alerts branches reconverging at the dashboard and the restyle touching five earlier surfaces.

global_rules.rule: Every percentage anywhere in the app (yields, gains, weights, and anything added later) is shown with exactly one decimal place and a % sign, like 4.2% — never 4.20% or 4%.
Wherever a stock appears anywhere in the app, its ticker is shown in a small navy badge in front of the company name, like [FJRD] Fjord Pharma.
Any list of stocks where the user has not chosen a sort defaults to alphabetical order by ticker, app-wide.

instruction: Please implement a sports analytics website that provides basketball betting data and analysis. The website should have functionalities for data visualization, match prediction, and betting recommendations. Users should be able to browse data for basketball, view match history, team rankings, player performance, and make informed betting decisions based on the analysis results. Define the background as ghost white and components as slate gray.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the sports data visualization section for basketball.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page displays graphical representations of sports data relevant to the basketball, such as charts or graphs, without any layout issues or missing data points.

ui_instruct.task: Access the match prediction feature for an upcoming game.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The match prediction page correctly shows predicted outcomes with percentage probabilities, based on current data and analysis, without any technical errors or missing information.

ui_instruct.task: Use the search function to find a specific team's historical match data.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The search results page displays a list of matches involving the specified team, sorted chronologically, with complete match details such as scores and dates.

ui_instruct.task: Check the team rankings page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page lists teams ranked according to their current standings, with clear markers indicating any ties, and contains accurate data consistent with known league standings.

ui_instruct.task: Evaluate the player performance section for individual stats.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The section shows detailed statistics for players, including metrics like goals, assists, and average ratings, with data clearly labeled and easy to interpret.

ui_instruct.task: Assess the betting recommendations provided for a specific match.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The recommendations offer actionable betting advice backed by data analysis, including relevant statistics or trends that support the suggestions.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'ghost white' as the background color and 'slate gray' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'ghost white' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'slate gray', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.source_feature: Odds Comparison Across Sportsbooks
follow_ups.instruction: Love the predictions, but I shop lines, so give me a proper odds board page with the weekend's games grouped Friday through Sunday. Load exactly these six, home side's moneyline listed in BetNova, HoopLine, CourtSide order (I'll wire real feeds later): Fri Celtics @ Knicks, our model has the Knicks at 58%, -130 / -125 / -135; Fri Lakers @ Bulls, Bulls 44%, +140 / +145 / +140; Sat Suns @ Heat, Heat 51%, -105 / -110 / -102; Sat Nuggets @ Raptors, Raptors 38%, +170 / +165 / +170; Sun Warriors @ Mavericks, Mavericks 62%, -150 / -155 / -148; Sun Bucks @ Hornets, Hornets 47%, +120 / +118 / +125. Highlight each game's best home price along with which book has it (if two books tie for best, flag them both), and show the implied win probability baked into that best price, to one decimal. Two house styles for everything in this app, now and for anything we add later: odds always in American form with the sign showing (+145, -125, never decimal), and matchups always written away team @ home team.

ui_instruct.task: Open the odds board and read the implied win probability shown for the Celtics @ Knicks game's best price.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It reads 55.6%, derived from the best home price of -125 at HoopLine — not 56.5%, which would mean it was computed from BetNova's -130.

ui_instruct.task: Find the Nuggets @ Raptors game on the odds board and look at how the best price is marked.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The +170 price is flagged as best at both BetNova and CourtSide — both books marked — while HoopLine's +165 is not marked as best.

ui_instruct.task: Look at the Warriors @ Mavericks game on the odds board.
ui_instruct.expected_result: CourtSide's -148 is highlighted as the best home price, not HoopLine's -155 — for negative American odds the number closest to even money is the better payout.

ui_instruct.task: Scan the six games on the odds board.

target_app_summary: The basketball prediction site grows into a full line-shopping and bet-management platform. A pinned six-game weekend odds board carrying the base model's win probabilities and home moneylines at three sportsbooks becomes the data spine: a parlay slip books legs at best prices, the base betting-recommendations feature is rebuilt into a Best Bets value-edge ranking, an adjustments panel lets users override model probabilities and re-rank the edges live, and watch alerts with typed target edges flip between fired and armed as those numbers move. A ticket-placement workflow with a bankroll feeds a Performance analytics page (ROI, records, singles-vs-parlays, a cent-locked settled-ticket ledger), while the base match-history lookup is upgraded into a matchup research center grading past meetings against closing lines with ATS/over-under records and push handling, deep-linked from the board. A final emerald rebrand sweeps every surface including the original rankings page. The graph roots at the base app: predictions -> board -> slip -> tickets -> performance (5 deep from T1) and board -> edge finder -> adjustments -> watch alerts.

global_rules.rule: Odds are always displayed in American form with an explicit sign (+145, -125), never as decimal odds, everywhere in the app.

follow_ups.source_feature: Module-level alert system
follow_ups.instruction: My Chimney 3 panel worries me, so build an alert center. There's a rules area where I type a yield threshold — any panel whose weekly yield lands strictly below it raises an alert, sitting at the number exactly is still fine, and it's one alert per panel even if a couple of rules catch it — plus an active alerts list and a separate resolved log, with each alert naming the panel and its yield. Start me with one rule at 25.0 already in place. When I acknowledge an alert, ask me to confirm first, then it moves to the resolved log, and show how many alerts are active right in the navigation. Oh, and from now on across the whole app: any status gets a colored dot plus a word next to it — red dot 'Active', green dot 'Resolved', that kind of thing — never color by itself.

ui_instruct.task: In the alert center's rules area, type 33.0 as a new rule threshold and add the rule.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly 3 alerts are active — Corner 2, Gable 1, and Chimney 3 — while Ridge East and Ridge West (sitting exactly at 33.0) are not flagged, Chimney 3 appears only once even though the pre-set 25.0 rule also catches it, and the navigation badge reads 3.

ui_instruct.task: Open the alert center on a fresh load and look at the active alerts list.
ui_instruct.expected_result: One alert is active — Chimney 3, caught by the pre-set 25.0 rule — shown with a red dot plus the word Active, and the navigation badge shows 1.

ui_instruct.task: Acknowledge the Chimney 3 alert and confirm when asked.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A confirmation step appears before anything moves; after confirming, Chimney 3 leaves the active list, shows up in the resolved log with a green dot plus the word Resolved, and the navigation badge drops to 0.

ui_instruct.task: Read the yield figure shown on Chimney 3's alert, then open the Panels page and find Chimney 3's row.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both show the same 18.0 yield, and Chimney 3 sits at the bottom of the panel ranking — consistent with it being the only panel below the 25.0 rule.

ui_instruct.task: On the savings calculator, type 0.30 into the electricity rate field and 9000 into the system cost field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Yearly savings show $982.02 (3,273.40 kWh x $0.30) and the payback reads 9 years, 2 months — the partial month rounds up, so not 9 years 1 month and not a bare decimal like 9.2 years.

follow_ups.source_feature: CSV Data Export
follow_ups.instruction: I keep retyping panel numbers into emails — give me a report builder. Let me tick which panels to include, with quick buttons for South, East, everything, and none, and render a plain-text report right on the page that I can copy: how many panels are in it, their combined output, the average yield — just average the panels' yield figures to one decimal, don't weight by panel size — and the best and worst panel by yield, going alphabetical on a tie. If nothing's ticked, say so nicely instead of showing zeros or NaN garbage, and the report should redo itself the moment I change the ticks.

ui_instruct.task: In the report builder, click the East quick button and read the generated report.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The report shows 3 panels, combined output 24.20 kWh, average yield 25.3 (the plain mean of 30.0, 28.0 and 18.0 — not the size-weighted 25.5), best panel Corner 2, worst panel Chimney 3.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The report shows 2 panels, combined output 24.75 kWh, and names Ridge East as the best panel — the 33.0 yield tie breaks alphabetically.

ui_instruct.expected_result: With nothing ticked a friendly empty message replaces the report — no zeros, NaN, or crash — and the report reappears the moment one panel is ticked.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Both read 62.95 kWh, and the report names Peak 1 as best and Chimney 3 as worst across all 6 panels.

ui_instruct.expected_result: South shows 38.75 kWh, East shows 24.20 kWh, and the fleet shows 62.95 kWh with a total rated capacity of 2,100 W — the two array totals sum exactly to the fleet total.

follow_ups.source_feature: Actual vs. Estimated Generation Comparison
follow_ups.instruction: How do I know the system's doing what it should? On the historical chart, add an expected-generation baseline I can toggle on: I type peak sun hours per day — start it at 5.0 — and expected comes from the fleet's rated capacity on the panels page times those hours, day by day. Show a performance number next to the chart, actual week over expected week as a percent to one decimal, with a health read beside it: 90 or better is Healthy, 75 up to 90 is Watch, under 75 is Fault. It should all move the instant I edit the hours.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The performance readout shows 85.6% (62.95 kWh actual vs 73.50 kWh expected for the week) with a Watch health read — not 85.7%, not 86%, and not Healthy or Fault.

follow_ups.instruction: Now show me the feel-good numbers: an environmental impact page. Take the fleet's weekly total from the panels page and turn it into CO2 avoided at 0.4 kg per kWh — this week's figure plus a projected year — and show the annual energy it rests on, which has to be the exact same weekly-times-52 number the savings calculator runs on. CO2 reads in kg with two decimals, but the moment a figure reaches 1,000 kg flip it to tonnes with two decimals instead of some four-digit kg monster. Give me a tree line too — figure one tree soaks up 21 kg of CO2 a year, divide the annual CO2 by that, and round down to whole trees, no fractional trees. And split this week's impact by array: South and East each with their kg and their percent share to one decimal, and those two shares better add up to 100.

follow_ups.source_feature: Power Flow Diagram
follow_ups.instruction: Now the fun one: a live power flow page — an animated diagram of panels, battery, home, and grid with the current number on each flow, in kW with two decimals. Give me three inputs to play with: sun level as a percent, home load in kW, and battery percent, defaulted to 60. Generation is the fleet's rated capacity from the panels page scaled by the sun level; surplus charges the battery until it hits 100 and then spills to the grid, while a shortfall drains the battery down to a 20 floor before pulling from the grid. Whatever I type, the numbers have to balance — what the panels make plus whatever the battery or grid chips in always matches what the home takes plus whatever's being stored or exported, live as I type.

ui_instruct.task: On the power flow page, type 100 into the sun level and 1.50 into the home load, leaving the battery at its default 60.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Generation reads 2.10 kW, the home takes 1.50 kW, the battery charges at 0.60 kW, and the grid shows 0.00 kW — the flows add up exactly.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Generation reads 1.05 kW and the 1.95 kW shortfall is covered by the battery discharging, with the grid at 0.00 kW — generation plus battery discharge equals the home's 3.00 kW.

ui_instruct.task: Type 100 into the battery percent, 100 into the sun level, and 1.00 into the home load.
ui_instruct.expected_result: With the battery already full, the 1.10 kW surplus flows entirely to the grid as export and the battery flow reads 0.00 kW.

follow_ups.source_feature: System Health Status Indicator
follow_ups.instruction: Bring it all together on a System Health page with one score. Start at 100, knock off 15 for every active alert in the alert center, and 10 more if the fleet's average yield — the plain average of the panels' yield figures — is under 30.0. 90 and up reads Healthy, 75 through 89 is Watch, below 75 is Fault, and I want the deductions listed out so I can see why, plus a to-do line for each active alert and one for low fleet yield if that's dinging me. When I go acknowledge an alert, the score should have caught up by the time I'm back on the page.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The score is 75 with a Watch health read (75 lands in Watch, not Fault), broken down as 100 minus 15 for the one active alert (Chimney 3) minus 10 because the fleet's average yield of 29.5 is under 30.0.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly two to-do lines show — one for the active Chimney 3 alert and one for the low fleet average yield — matching the two deductions in the breakdown.

ui_instruct.task: Compare the displayed score with the deduction lines on the System Health page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The score equals 100 minus the sum of the listed deductions — the breakdown shown is internally consistent with the headline number.

ui_instruct.task: Go to the alert center, acknowledge the Chimney 3 alert and confirm, then return to the System Health page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The score rises to exactly 90 with a Healthy read (90 is the Healthy boundary), and the to-do list drops to a single line about the low fleet yield.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The weekly figure reads 25.18 kg (62.95 kWh x 0.4) and the annual projection reads 1.31 t — the 1,309.36 kg crosses the 1,000 kg line so it shows in tonnes with two decimals, not as 1,309.36 kg and not rounded to 1.3 t.

target_app_summary: The solar dashboard has grown into a full home-solar operations platform. A panel fleet registry with per-array rollups and yield rankings became the backbone: it feeds a live-typing savings and payback calculator, a threshold-based alert workflow with rules, an active list and a resolved log, a copyable panel report builder, an expected-vs-actual performance overlay on the historical chart, an environmental impact page that converts fleet output into CO2 avoided and tree equivalents, a physics-honest power flow simulator, and finally a System Health score that reconciles the alert center and fleet yields into one graded number with to-dos. A design refresh mid-way moved the whole app from honeydew to a cream-and-amber card system. The graph is hub-and-spoke around the registry (T2, itself built off the base dashboard, feeds every later turn) with one deep chain rooted at the base — base to registry to alert center to health score — so early breakage compounds; three app-wide conventions (two-decimal kWh, invalid-input-never-blanks, dot-plus-word statuses) are tested silently on every new surface.

global_rules.rule: Energy values are always displayed as kWh with exactly two decimals (9.00 kWh, 62.95 kWh) everywhere in the app.
Invalid input never blanks a result anywhere: the last valid output stays on screen alongside a small note about the bad input.
Every status or health indicator is a colored dot plus a word (red dot 'Active', green dot 'Resolved'), never color alone.

instruction: Please implement a text-based strategy browser game where players can choose a race, manage resources, upgrade, and battle. The game should have multiple pages, including the base page, ranking page, store, train page, workers page, upgrades page, bank page, messages page, and reports page. Players can choose from four races: Humans, Dragonborns, Elves, and Dwarfs, each with unique attributes. Players can manage resources, including gold, iron, wood, and wheat, and can upgrade their city, workers, and soldiers. Design the site using seashell as the background and crimson for content blocks.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Each click on a race should display specific attributes unique to that race, and the selection should be confirmed on the page.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The selected item should be removed from the store and added to your inventory, with the appropriate deduction in resources.

ui_instruct.task: Access the "Train Page" and begin training workers or soldiers.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Training should commence with a status update visible, and there should be an indication of resource consumption related to this activity.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the "Workers Page" and assign a task to workers.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The task should be acknowledged by the system with relevant feedback on expected completion, and any resource costs should be visibly deducted.

ui_instruct.task: Visit the "Upgrades Page" and attempt to upgrade a soldier.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The upgrade should succeed, show updated soldier stats, and the necessary resources should be spent.

ui_instruct.task: Access the "Bank Page" and deposit gold.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The deposited gold should reflect in the bank balance, deducting from available on-hand funds with confirmation of the transaction.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'seashell' as the background color and 'crimson' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'seashell' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'crimson', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.instruction: The bank page is dead weight right now — put a proper merchant exchange in it. Set my stockpile to exactly 2,500 gold, 1,800 iron, 1,200 wood and 900 wheat, and let me trade iron, wood or wheat into gold at 3 iron, 4 wood or 5 wheat per gold piece, with the merchant skimming 10% — take his cut before rounding and always round down to whole gold, so 100 iron should come out to 30 gold, not 29. The gold preview has to update live while I'm typing the amount, and it should refuse negatives, junk input, or any amount over what I actually hold. And a house rule for this whole game, now and for anything we add later: any action that spends or converts my resources shows me the exact numbers first and waits for my confirm.

follow_ups.instruction: Build me a battle simulator page that replays the whole fight live with every keystroke — no submit button, the projection just regenerates as I type. I enter my attacker count, the defender count, and a luck percent anywhere from -25 to 25 (anything outside that range or not a number gets refused with a message). Morale is defenders divided by attackers times 100, rounded and clamped between 30 and 100, worked out once from the counts I typed — and show it in the projection. The fight then plays out in rounds until one side is wiped out: each round the defenders lose a quarter of my current effective strength rounded up — that's my remaining attackers times morale-over-100 times (1 + luck/100) — while I lose a quarter of their current count with its flat 10% defense bonus, rounded up. Both hits land in the same round, and if both sides reach zero together the defenders hold the field. Show me the whole round-by-round casualty log with the counts left standing, ending in the outcome, rounds fought and survivors. Zero defenders is just an instant walkover win before any morale math runs — don't let the division blow up. target_app_summary: The text-based strategy game has grown from a resource-and-battle skeleton into a full empire sim. The bank became a live merchant exchange with cut-before-round conversion math; the reports page became a seeded war chronicle whose six pinned battles feed almost everything downstream: salvage expeditions harvest debris from its victories, a Hall of Plaques tiers its aggregates, a round-by-round battle simulator pre-fills rematches from its opponents, alliance join letters quote its record, and a power score counts its victories. On top sit alliance diplomacy with tagged rivals on the ranking, a Territories module whose outposts re-sort the ranking live with alphabetical tiebreaks, a royal war-room restyle unifying five pages, and a Herald's Proclamation composer that publishes a live-valued summary of the chronicle, plaques, power/rank and alliance state to the messages page. The feature graph is hub-shaped around the chronicle (T3) with two chains three deep (T1-T3-T5-T10 and T1-T3-T9-T10).

follow_ups.instruction: The tracker tells clients where each case sits, but not what to actually do next — so add a Dispute Strategy Advisor page. It reads the tracker as it stands right now, never a stale snapshot, and rolls the cases up by creditor: Midland gets one card even though we're fighting them at two bureaus. Each creditor card works out the next move — if any of their cases is still a Draft, it says 'Send the pending letter'; otherwise if anything's Sent, 'Await the bureau's response'; and once everything with that creditor is Resolved, 'Request an updated credit report'. Rank the cards by a priority score shown on the card: 2 points for every case of theirs that isn't resolved yet, plus a 3-point bonus when we're disputing them at more than one bureau — tag those cards 'multi-bureau' — and break ties alphabetically by creditor name. Change a case over in the tracker and the advisor better show it the moment you come back.

target_app_summary: What began as an old-lace-and-rosy-brown lead-gen brochure site for a credit repair company has grown into a full client acquisition and service portal. Discovery and conversion now run through a live score-improvement estimator wired to the original credit score inquiry, a tie-aware filterable success-stories directory, and a checkout-style plan enrollment flow that inherits the estimator's plan recommendation. Service delivery grew its own arm rooted in the original lead form: the form's submitted name auto-signs the dispute letter builder's letters, saved letters feed a Draft/Sent/Resolved dispute tracker, and the tracker in turn drives both an impact dashboard and a per-creditor dispute strategy advisor that rolls cases up by creditor, ranks them by a priority score with a multi-bureau bonus, and derives each creditor's next move. A consultation scheduler with per-advisor slot availability and a site-wide brand restyle round it out. The feature graph has one deep service chain (lead form -> letter builder -> tracker -> dashboard/advisor), a conversion chain (inquiry -> estimator -> enrollment), and three silent app-wide conventions (score band labels, '+N pts' gain formatting, Start-over resets) tested across every new surface.

edges.what: inquiry's captured score prefills the estimator
lead form's submitted name auto-signs the generated dispute letters
saved letters become Draft dispute cases
aggregates the seven pinned success stories
items-resolved stat counts tracker's resolved cases live
restyles home page and lead form
restyles estimator page
restyles success stories page and plan badges
restyles letter builder page
restyles dispute tracker and status badges
restyles impact dashboard page
estimator's plan recommendation preselects the enrollment plan
advisor rolls live tracker cases into per-creditor next actions and priority rankings

global_rules.rule: Every displayed credit score carries its band label next to it — under 580 Poor, 580-669 Fair, 670-739 Good, 740-799 Very Good, 800+ Excellent — e.g. '612 (Fair)'.
Every form or tool surface keeps a visible 'Start over' control that resets it to its initial blank state.
Score gains always render with a leading plus sign and 'pts' suffix, e.g. '+84 pts'.

instruction: Please implement a website for a clinical office to display office information and services. The website should have basic pages, including a homepage, about us, services, and contact us. Users should be able to browse the website, learn about the office's information, view the services provided, and contact the office through the contact page. The website should also have a simple navigation menu to help users quickly find the information they need. Style all pages with a light cyan background and cadet blue components.

Each card should show all of that, with the most experienced doctors first — and when two tie on years just go alphabetically by last name, so Natarajan sits ahead of Reyes and Vasquez ahead of Webb, even though that's not how I listed them. Give me specialty filter buttons up top, and a badge on each card for accepting-new-patients versus waitlist-only. follow_ups.source_feature: Office hours displayed with after-hours contact
follow_ups.instruction: Next up: a Plan Your Visit page. target_app_summary: What started as a simple house-cleaning brochure site (booking, inquiry, status check, contact) has grown into a full service-business platform. Discovery and pricing grew an instant quote estimator over a fixed six-package catalog, a ZIP-based service-area checker that feeds travel fees into quotes, and a side-by-side package comparison table. Commerce grew a gift-certificate store with a balance ledger, a quote-to-checkout booking flow with certificate redemption math, and a membership plans configurator with recurring discounts. Social proof lives in a filterable reviews hub whose averages feed both the comparison table and an owner-facing Business Snapshot dashboard that rolls up booked revenue, outstanding certificate balances, and overall rating. A site-wide restyle (deep teal actions, bordered cards, uppercase headings, golden stars) unifies the grown surface area. The feature graph has one deep spine (estimator -> area fees -> checkout -> dashboard) plus reviews and certificates each feeding two downstream consumers.

target_app_summary: The All-In Bourbon Bar's brochure site has grown into a full club platform. Discovery grew a multi-criteria Bourbon Library screener that feeds an interactive Build-a-Flight tool and a rated Tasting Journal with a Top Shelf leaderboard. The poker side grew a tournament calendar with a real registration workflow, a one-click Guest Pass night board with claim caps and cancellations that reopen sold-out nights, all respecting tournament blackout nights, and a capstone Night Out Planner that assembles tournaments, saved flights, and plus-one passes into one costed, points-previewed itinerary. Commerce and loyalty grew a denomination-pick gift card studio with printed bonus tiers and a per-keystroke card preview and a Player's Ledger that rolls flights, registrations, and card purchases into a tiered points balance, and a site-wide 'card table' restyle unified the look. The graph's spine is T1->T2->T4->T7->T10, with the ledger (T7) fanning in from three earlier features and the planner (T10) fanning in from four.

target_app_summary: The base lead-management CRM grows into a full sales platform. Discovery and prioritization come from an engagement scoring engine with per-lead activity logs (pinned six-lead seed) and later an Inbox/Pipeline triage split fed by a lead-capture form builder. instruction: Please implement a technical website to display technical information and solutions. The website should have functionalities for browsing technical articles, searching technical information, and viewing solutions. Users should be able to browse technical articles, search technical information, view solutions, and communicate with other users.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the technical articles section using the main navigation menu.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The technical articles section loads correctly, displaying available articles with a clear and accessible layout.

ui_instruct.task: Use the search functionality to find a specific technical topic.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Relevant search results are displayed matching the query, and the results are relevant to technical information.

ui_instruct.task: Open a technical article and verify its content.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The article loads without errors and the content displayed is technical in nature, accurate, and complete based on the article’s title.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'lavender' as the background color and 'indigo' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'lavender' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'indigo', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.instruction: The article list needs a proper screener, not just that search box. Start me off with exactly these six articles, I'll add more later: 'Taming React Re-renders' by Priya Nair (Web Development, #react #performance, Advanced, 8,400 views all-time with 320 this week, 1,800 words); 'SQL Indexing Demystified' by Marcus Webb (Databases, #sql #performance, Intermediate, 12,100 views with 150 this week, 1,200 words); 'Intro to Binary Trees' by Priya Nair (Algorithms, #datastructures, Beginner, 3,300 views with 540 this week, 900 words); 'Debugging Memory Leaks in Node' by Elena Fox (Web Development, #node #performance, Advanced, 6,750 views with 540 this week, 2,100 words); 'REST vs GraphQL' by Marcus Webb (Web Development, #api, Intermediate, 15,600 views with 90 this week, 1,500 words); and 'Understanding TCP Handshakes' by Elena Fox (Networking, #networking, Beginner, 980 views with 210 this week, 600 words). I want a category picker, clickable tag chips, and a minimum-views box I can type a number into — picking two tags should widen things (either tag matches) but the other controls narrow (category AND tags AND views), with a live count of matches, plus let me save a filter combo under a name and pull it back later, and a sort control for all-time views, this week's views, or title, where tied view counts fall back to alphabetical by title. Oh and two things I want everywhere in this app from now on, including anything we add later: view counts of a thousand or more get shortened like 12.1k (one decimal), and anything with a difficulty level wears a colored badge — green for Beginner, amber for Intermediate, red for Advanced.

target_app_summary: The little technical-articles site grows into a full developer knowledge hub. Discovery gets deep: a multi-criteria article screener with saved presets and tie-aware sorting, plus a Trending This Week dashboard that scores articles from weekly views and emoji reactions. Community output becomes first-class: an emoji reaction system, a validated multi-step Share-a-Solution publishing flow, a contributor level system where reactions received and published solutions jointly gate Reader/Rising/Expert/Legend tiers (both conditions required, so the most-reacted author can still sit at Rising), and a curated Featured Queue that feeds the homepage. Personal tooling arrives with a bookmark-driven Reading List with rounded-up read times and progress tracking, and everything is capped by a Weekly Digest builder that auto-assembles trending, featured, and contributor-spotlight content behind per-section include/exclude toggles into a publishable digest with a live-rebuilding plain-text copy block. A mid-ladder site-wide restyle (dark slate header, teal actions, difficulty-colored card accents) must land consistently on every earlier surface. The feature graph runs deep: reactions feed trending, trending feeds the featured queue, and trending + featured + contributor levels all converge in the digest (T1->T3->T5->T8->T10).

target_app_summary: The anonymous campus forum grows into a full campus community platform. Discovery gets serious: an up/down voting system with net scores and tie-aware Top/New sorting feeds a windowed Trending tab, a multi-criteria screener with saved presets, and a publishable Campus Digest that snapshots trending posts and marketplace deals into frozen editions. Community tooling arrives via attachable opinion polls with live one-decimal percentage bars, per-thread emoji personas with an optional identity-reveal signature, and a report-driven Moderation Queue whose auto-flagging fires off vote-score thresholds. A three-step Marketplace adds practical campus utility with validated listings, category badges and price sorting. A final design pass unifies feed, Trending, Marketplace and Moderation Queue under one pill-badge, accent-stripe, signed-score visual language. The graph runs deep: voting (T2) powers Trending (T4), the screener (T6) and moderation auto-flagging (T7), while the Digest (T9) aggregates Trending and Marketplace output — a 3-deep chain T1-T2-T4-T9.

Every count in the app is correctly pluralized ('1 vote' / '2 votes', '1 match', '1 report') — never '1 votes' — everywhere, forever.

target_app_summary: The base beige-and-saddle-brown Q&A site grows into a full community knowledge platform. A pinned seven-question seed powers a tag screener with boolean tag/status filtering and tie-aware score sorting; an ask composer adds live duplicate detection and strict validation; an accept-answer workflow introduces a Solved state that propagates into the screener, a Topics analytics hub, and a capstone Triage dashboard. A points-based bounty system feeds a Featured strip, the follow-and-digest builder, and the Triage urgency ranking, while an edit-suggestion review queue adds moderation whose pending count also lands on Triage. A site-wide restyle pass locks visual consistency across the screener, Topics, Review, and Digest pages. The graph runs several chains three-plus deep (base list -> screener -> bounties -> triage; base answers -> accept workflow -> topics/triage), so early breakage compounds.

follow_ups.instruction: Sellers keep nagging me about actually getting paid out, so build a Payout Center. It has a seller picker: I choose a seller and see their lifetime earned - for each of their Released trades in the ledger, the gross amount minus our 0.75% seller-side fee from the fee schedule, with Refunded, Disputed and In Escrow trades contributing nothing - plus what's pending or already paid, and what's available right now. From there the seller requests a withdrawal by typing an amount: refuse anything over the available balance and anything under $250, and the moment a request goes through it puts a hold on that money so available drops right away. Requests land in a pending queue on an admin approvals page where I approve or reject each one - approving moves it to a paid history list, rejecting lifts the hold and puts the money back in available. And a house rule starting now: anything anywhere in this app that moves or releases money has to show me a confirmation with the exact dollar amounts before it happens - that goes for everything we add later too.

follow_ups.instruction: Buyers keep telling me the asks on the screener are close but not quite right, so let them haggle. Every offer on the Offer Screener gets a Negotiate button that opens a little console showing that offer's ask price per coin and its size, with a box where I type my proposed price per coin. Every keystroke updates three readouts on the spot: my discount off that offer's ask as a percentage to two decimals - measured against the ask itself, not the coin's reference price - the total the deal would come to at my price, and what the seller would pocket from that total after their 0.75% fee share. Proposed prices at or above the ask make no sense, and more than 10% below the ask is insulting - in both cases show a warning and keep the send button dead, though exactly 10% below is still fair game. Sending a counter parks it on the offer where the seller can see it and accept, and accepting swaps the offer's screener price to the agreed number and re-sorts the board.

target_app_summary: The base crypto escrow marketplace has grown into a full P2P trading platform. It gained a live fee-and-payout calculator, a platform-wide Trade Ledger with released/locked rollups seeded with eight pinned trades, a seller Payout Center with fee-netted lifetime earnings and a hold-then-approve withdrawal queue, a seller reputation leaderboard with refund penalties and volume tiebreaks, a sandboxed practice mode with a mock wallet and its own seeded practice listings, a multi-criteria offer screener with saved presets and a reputation filter, a per-keystroke counter-offer negotiation console that re-prices screener offers, a brand restyle across five pages, and copyable seller statements that reconcile ledger records against the fee schedule and the Payout Center. The ledger (T3) is the hub: payout balances and reputation scores are computed from it, practice mode must leave it untouched, and statements are generated from it; the fee schedule (T2) feeds the Payout Center, the negotiation console, and the statements; reputation chains into the screener and the screener into the negotiation console, giving deep chains like T1->T3->T5->T7->T8 and T1->T3->T4->T10.

global_rules.rule: Crypto amounts are always shown to exactly 8 decimal places with the ticker after the number (e.g. 0.16666667 BTC), and dollar figures always as $1,234.56 with commas and two decimals.
Every trade status is a color-coded pill badge everywhere: amber In Escrow, green Released, gray Refunded, dark red Disputed.
Any action that moves or releases funds shows a confirmation with the exact dollar amounts before it completes.

instruction: Please implement an online trading website for bidding and trading. The website should have functionalities for bidding and trading, allowing users to browse trading opportunities, place orders, manage their trading accounts, and view their trading history. Set the background color to lemon chiffon and the component color to chocolate.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the bidding section and place a bid on a trading opportunity.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The bid is successfully placed and reflected in the user's bid history, with all relevant details accurately recorded.

ui_instruct.task: Browse the available trading opportunities on the website.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A comprehensive list of trading opportunities is displayed, relevant to the user's preferences, without any missing or irrelevant entries.

ui_instruct.task: View the user's trading history from the account dashboard.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A detailed and accurate history of all past trading and bidding activities is displayed, including dates and transaction details.

ui_instruct.task: Update account information via the account management page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The information is updated successfully, and a confirmation message is displayed, with changes reflected correctly on subsequent views.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'lemon chiffon' as the background color and 'chocolate' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'lemon chiffon' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'chocolate', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.source_feature: Saved searches / followed searches
follow_ups.instruction: The browse page is getting crowded — build me a proper screener for the catalog. Start me off with exactly these seven listings, I'll grow it later: 1968 Rolex Submariner (Collectibles, current bid $4,200.00, +5.25% this session, 12 bids, seller Harbor Trade Co, Open, closes July 21), 10oz Silver Bullion Bar (Metals, $310.00, -1.10%, 4 bids, MetalWorks, Open, closes July 18), Signed First-Edition Dune (Collectibles, $850.00, +5.25%, 7 bids, PageTurners, Open, closes July 25), Antique Oak Writing Desk (Furniture, $1,150.00, -0.40%, 9 bids, Harbor Trade Co, Closing, closes July 17), Gold Krugerrand Coin (Metals, $2,050.00, +2.75%, 15 bids, MetalWorks, Open, closes July 30), Persian Heriz Rug (Furniture, $980.00, -3.60%, 2 bids, Attic Finds, Open, closes July 22), and 1974 Fender Stratocaster (Collectibles, $3,300.00, +6.40%, 21 bids, Attic Finds, already Settled). I want category checkboxes where ticking two means show either one, typed min and max price boxes and a status picker that all narrow together, a live match counter that always agrees with what's actually on screen, and a way to save a filter combo under a name and load it back later. Two things I care about everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: session changes always display signed with two decimals like +5.25% or -1.10%, and a listing's status always shows as a colored pill — green for Open, amber for Closing, gray for Settled.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, check the Collectibles and Metals category boxes, type 800 into the minimum price field, and set the status filter to Open.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly three listings show: 1968 Rolex Submariner, Signed First-Edition Dune, and Gold Krugerrand Coin — the 1974 Fender Stratocaster stays hidden even though it's a Collectible over $800, because it's Settled.

ui_instruct.task: Check only the Metals category box on the screener, then additionally check the Furniture box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: With Metals alone the live match counter reads 2 with exactly the 10oz Silver Bullion Bar and Gold Krugerrand Coin visible; after adding Furniture the counter reads 4 and both furniture listings join the results — categories combine as either-or, not both-and.

ui_instruct.task: With only the Metals box checked, save the search as a preset named 'Metals watch', clear all filters, then load the 'Metals watch' preset.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Clearing filters brings back all 7 listings; loading the preset re-applies the Metals filter and the results return to exactly the 10oz Silver Bullion Bar and Gold Krugerrand Coin.

ui_instruct.task: Filter the screener to the Metals category, open the 10oz Silver Bullion Bar listing, place a bid of 360, then open the trading history.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The 360 bid on the 10oz Silver Bullion Bar appears as a new entry in the trading history.

ui_instruct.task: Open the trading history section of the account area.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A trading history view renders without errors, showing past trading and bidding activity (or a sensible empty state if nothing has happened yet).

follow_ups.source_feature: Auction countdown timer per listing (reshaped into close-state-aware final-bid mechanics)
follow_ups.instruction: Bidding feels like a black box — give every listing a proper bid ticket. As I type an amount it should live-calculate the 12.5% buyer's premium, the flat $25.00 handling fee, and the total due, rounded to the cent with half-cents rounding up. Enforce increments too: a bid has to top the current bid by at least $50 while the current bid is under $1,000, and by at least $100 once it's $1,000 or more — and tell me the exact floor when I'm short. One more habit I want everywhere in this app from now on, for anything that commits money or can't be undone: show me a summary to confirm before it goes through, starting with this ticket, whose confirmed bids land in my trading history like always. And Settled listings shouldn't accept bids at all.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Before any submit, the ticket live-shows a buyer's premium of $113.13, a $25.00 handling fee, and a total due of $1,043.13 — the half-cent on the premium rounds up, so $113.13 rather than $113.12.

ui_instruct.task: Open the bid ticket on the Gold Krugerrand Coin, type 2100, then change it to 2150.
ui_instruct.expected_result: 2100 is rejected with a message about the $100 minimum increment (current bid is $2,050.00 so the floor is $2,150.00) and cannot be submitted; changing to 2150 clears the error and the ticket becomes submittable.

ui_instruct.task: On the Signed First-Edition Dune bid ticket, type 900, then delete the amount so the field is empty.
ui_instruct.expected_result: While 900 is typed the total due reads $1,037.50 without submitting anything; once the field is emptied the ticket falls back to a calm neutral state — no NaN, no crash, no stale total left behind.

ui_instruct.task: Bid 360 on the 10oz Silver Bullion Bar through the ticket, go through the confirmation step, then open the trading history.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A confirmation summary appears first showing the $360.00 bid and the $430.00 total due; after confirming, the bid shows up in the trading history.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, check the Collectibles and Metals category boxes, type 800 into the minimum price field, and set the status filter to Open.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly three listings show: 1968 Rolex Submariner, Signed First-Edition Dune, and Gold Krugerrand Coin — the 1974 Fender Stratocaster stays hidden even though it's a Collectible over $800, because it's Settled.

follow_ups.source_feature: Price results / past sales lookup (extended into the settlement workflow that produces the results)
follow_ups.instruction: Time to actually close auctions. Backfill some history for me: PageTurners has three past sales reviewed at 5, 5 and 4 stars; MetalWorks two at 5 and 4; Harbor Trade Co a Georgian Side Table reviewed at 3 stars plus a Regency Mantel Clock sale at a $640.00 hammer that nobody has reviewed yet; and the Fender sale carries a 4-star review. follow_ups.instruction: The lemon-chiffon look has run its course — sharpen the whole thing up, same pages, new skin. target_app_summary: The little lemon-chiffon bidding site has grown into a full auction-trading platform. Discovery got serious: a multi-criteria screener with saved presets over a pinned seven-lot catalog, a starred watchlist with live value rollups, a Market Movers panel with tie-aware rankings, and a July 2026 close-date calendar that cross-filters by category and watchlist. Trading mechanics deepened: a live bid ticket computes tiered increments and fee-inclusive totals per keystroke, and a close-and-settle workflow turns Closing lots into searchable Completed Sales records using the same fee schedule. Community and context layers sit on top — seller profiles with half-up-rounded ratings and a tie-broken leaderboard gated on settled sales, and per-listing price-history charts with windowed high/low stats — before a final chocolate-pill restyle sweeps every surface. The feature graph runs one deep chain (bid ticket -> settlement -> reputation) alongside a discovery cluster (screener -> watchlist -> calendar) and movers fed by ticket activity.

target_app_summary: The base email composer has grown into a full email-operations suite. Around the original compose/send/templates core, it gained a seeded Delivery Log with status badges and combined status+search filtering, a Blocklist that live-validates and gates every send, an Analytics page computing open/bounce rates and a tie-broken opens leaderboard from the log, a Scheduled-send Outbox with a pinned platform clock that dispatches into the log, a per-keystroke personalization preview that pulls sample recipients from the log, an A/B subject-test wizard whose audience is the deduped log minus the blocklist, a segment builder computing saved audiences from log engagement minus the blocklist that feeds compose, a full design restyle across all surfaces, and a live copyable account Digest that reconciles the log, analytics, blocklist, outbox, and segments. The feature graph funnels through the Delivery Log (five consumers) and the Blocklist (three consumers), with the deepest chain running compose -> log -> analytics -> digest.

follow_ups.instruction: Something that's been biting us: partner data leaves holes in the custody chain, so I want a Chain Audit page that sweeps every product's journey in the registry and surfaces the gaps. Two things count as an issue: a Delivered event with no Shipped event anywhere before it (the shipping leg got skipped), and any event dated after a product was already Delivered (activity after delivery). Each issue entry names the product, says which rule it broke, and cites the offending event with its location and date. Arrange the whole page by lot: lots carrying issues float to the top ordered by how many issues they hold, alphabetical by lot number on ties, and clean lots sit underneath with a clean badge. It has to stay honest as data flows in - anything the bulk importer commits gets re-audited the moment it lands. And to be clear, a product sitting at Flagged is not by itself an audit issue: flags are a status problem, custody gaps are a data problem.

target_app_summary: The base traceability site (register products, track circulation, inquire status, verify authenticity, view stats) grows into a full supply-chain integrity platform. Operations gains lot-level grouping with rolled-up lot statuses, a validating bulk event importer that feeds product journeys, and a lot-scoped recall workflow with retrieval progress and auto-close. Anti-counterfeit tooling adds a scan monitor that logs every verification check and flags 7-day scan bursts against a typed threshold, plus a counterfeit report intake and investigation queue that uses the scan log as evidence and can flip products (and their lots) to Flagged. Discovery and quality surfaces add a multi-criteria registry screener with any-of status logic, presets and an on-page text export, a chain integrity audit that sweeps every journey for custody gaps (skipped shipping legs, activity after delivery) and ranks lots by issue count with clean badges, and a checkpoint analytics page that dedups products per location and ranks with alphabetical tie-breaks. A mid-ladder restyle unifies five surfaces under one firebrick-on-misty-rose skin. The graph runs deep: lots feed recalls and every lot-grouped rollup, and the importer feeds lot rollups, the integrity audit, and checkpoint analytics.

The system should have functionalities for office management, infrastructure management, procurement management, personnel management, financial management, and decision-making management. Users should be able to browse related information, submit applications, approve, query status, and perform related operations. The system should also include functions such as leave, middle-level cadres leaving Shenzhen, attendance, and "five powers" management, which can design and circulate corresponding forms and processes. target_app_summary: The base e-government portal grows into a full municipal resource-planning suite centered on a live budget-lines ledger. Procurement gains a keystroke-live requisition builder with budget validation and approval tiers, plus a supplier-facing vendor portal with quote tie-breaking and awards. Finance gains a travel-and-expense approval workflow that posts approved spending onto the ledger, a grants module with over-spend guards, and a what-if scenario planner that clones live spending. Decision-making gains a utilization/variance report with tie-aware ranking and rounding-sensitive rollups, a KPI dashboard whose statuses are computed against budget-line utilization, and a council decision-packet workflow that compiles the report, the KPI tallies, and council-tier procurement items into a reviewable, approvable brief. The feature graph runs a deep spine (budget lines -> expense posting -> utilization report -> decision packets) with the planner, KPI dashboard, and vendor portal branching off the same spine, and a mid-ladder restyle sweeping every surface.

target_app_summary: The base time-attendance app grows into a full workforce operations suite for a small company. A pinned six-person roster with an exact seeded week of hours (Mar 2-7, 2026) feeds a ranked weekly rollup, an overtime/exceptions board, a live pay-stub calculator, a filterable payroll report with on-screen export, and a schedule-adherence scoreboard. Around that analytics core sit workflows and tools: a PIN kiosk that punches straight into timesheets, a PTO/leave center with request-approve-deduct mechanics, and a punch-correction queue whose approvals rewrite timesheet days and cascade through the rollup and overtime flags. The graph runs deep: roster/timesheets (T2) feed overtime (T4) which feeds payroll (T6) and correction propagation (T8), while leave (T5) feeds both the report export (T7) and adherence scoring (T9); a final restyle (T10) sweeps six surfaces. App-wide conventions - 'Xh Ym' durations, 'Mon, Mar 2' dates, and confirm-before-approve/reject - are introduced early and silently enforced on every later surface.

Start me off with exactly these eight so I can play, and keep the roster in exactly the order I'm giving them — it's the order the paper forms got typed up, so it's on purpose not sorted by ID: WHS-1004 (45-59, White, wellness 6.4, Week 2), WHS-1001 (18-29, Hispanic, 6.4, Week 1), WHS-1002 (30-44, Black, 8.2, Week 1), WHS-1003 (30-44, Asian, 5.0, Week 2), WHS-1005 (18-29, Black, 9.1, Week 3), WHS-1006 (60+, Hispanic, 4.8, Week 3), WHS-1007 (45-59, Black, 6.4, Week 4), WHS-1008 (30-44, White, 7.6, Week 4) — exactly these, I'll add more later.
